claim: Support that helps low-knowledge learners is neutral or harmful for high-knowledge learners. Meta-analysis, full text read (Tetzlaff 2025): 60 studies, 176 effects, 5,924 people; novices d=+0.505 (95% CI 0.260 to 0.750), experts d=-0.428 (CI -0.647 to -0.209), difference d=0.971. Heterogeneity is very high (I2 about 88 to 91%); Egger tests show no publication bias; the effect is asymmetric (novice benefit larger).
agent_test: Run the schema on the same tasks with high vs low scaffold at equal tokens, split by baseline pass rate of the model; expect a crossover.
note: One meta-analysis, but it pools 60 studies from 35 journals. Few moderator cells; 2 databases.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Founding experiments show the crossover in industrial and technical tasks: novices d=+0.90 to +1.89, experts d=-0.31 to -0.88 (Kalyuga 1998, 2000, 2001; Tuovinen and Sweller; Kalyuga and Sweller 2004). Effect sizes were recomputed by Kalyuga (2007), small N (15-63 per cell), same research network.
agent_test: Reanalyse any prior ablation of the agent by difficulty tercile; look for a sign change of the scaffold effect.

claim: The reversal is often partial: in several studies the expert effect is near zero, not negative, so 'wasteful' is more common than 'harmful'.
agent_test: Measure scaffold effect with CI on strong-baseline items; test whether it is below zero or only zero.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Fading alone did not beat a good fixed alternative for everyone: in Reisslein et al. 2006 novices did better with example-problem pairs than with faded worked examples (d 0.28) while experts did better with faded examples (d -0.26 for example-problem pairs); adaptive fading of worked steps beat fixed fading in Salden et al. 2010 (abstract only).
agent_test: Compare fixed scaffold, scheduled fade, and pass-rate-triggered fade at equal tokens.
audit_note: Direction misread: Kalyuga's review table gives example-problem vs faded d = 0.28 for novices and -0.26 for experts, and says experts benefited more from faded examples and problem-example pairs, so faded examples were NOT worse than example-problem pairs for experts (they were worse for novices).
claim_before_audit: Fading worked steps is the proposed fix, but fading alone did not beat a good fixed alternative: faded examples (novice d 0.28, expert -0.26) were still worse than example-problem pairs for experts in Reisslein 2006; adaptive task selection beat fixed fading in Salden 2010 (abstract only).

claim: Learner-adapted instruction beat non-adapted instruction in several studies reviewed by Kalyuga (2007): knowledge gain effect sizes 0.46 (Kalyuga and Sweller 2004), 0.55 (2005) and 0.58 (Salden et al. 2006); Corbalan et al. 2006 found shared control better than system-controlled adaptive selection (posttest 0.25, cognitive load 0.37).
agent_test: Adaptive-vs-fixed scaffold arm; success is a gain at equal tokens, not just fewer tokens.
audit_note: Effect sizes 0.46, 0.55, 0.58, 0.25/0.37 match Kalyuga's 2007 review, but Corbalan's 0.37 load reduction compares shared control with fully system-controlled (also adaptive) selection, not with fixed instruction; the review is mostly the authors' own lab; the Seufert line is a different effect and not support.
claim_before_audit: Learner-tailored (adaptive) instruction gives small to medium gains over fixed instruction: knowledge gain 0.46-0.58, load reduction 0.37 (Kalyuga and Sweller 2004, 2005; Salden 2006; Corbalan 2006).

claim: Tests of prior-knowledge interactions often come out null or partial: no prior-knowledge x phase interaction in 136 graduate students (median split; sample met the 125 needed by the authors' power analysis), no effect of pretest in 63 pharmacy-technician students (Gure et al., abstract-level), and prior-knowledge moderation on only one of three outcomes (comprehension, three-way interaction) with N=102 (Herold and Seufert 2025).
agent_test: Pre-register interaction tests with enough items; use a continuous baseline, not a median split.
audit_note: The 136 study met its own power target (n=125 needed) so it is not an underpowered null, the N=36 'no differences' case has no listed source, and the apprentice study (Gure et al.) is a scaffold-style comparison whose interaction test was not seen in the abstract.
claim_before_audit: Interaction tests for the effect are often underpowered or fail: a null in 136 graduate students (median split), no pretest interaction in N=63 apprentices, moderation on only one of three outcomes with N=102, no differences in N=36.

claim: Element interactivity is a rival account: the reversal appears with high-interactivity material and shrinks or vanishes with low-interactivity material (Chen, Kalyuga and Sweller 2017; Blayney 2016; Chen, Retnowati and Kalyuga 2020). Only abstracts were read. Tetzlaff 2025 did not code element interactivity; it cites it as one post-hoc reading of the weak primary-school effect (d19).
agent_test: Tag tasks by number of interacting steps; test whether the scaffold effect depends on that rather than on model strength.

claim: Curated procedural help raises agent pass rates on average (SkillsBench v4: 33.9% to 50.5%, +16.6 pp, 87 tasks, 18 configurations) but 13 of 87 tasks got worse (largest -7.4 pp). Re-checked against arXiv v4. The paper gives no text table of per-task baseline against delta; it explains negatives by skill design (heavy pipeline, displaced native strategy, brittle solver) and 3-trial noise is large (d25).
agent_test: Per-task help delta vs model baseline; check whether negative deltas cluster on high-baseline tasks.

claim: Stronger baseline does not cleanly mean smaller lift in agents: Gemini 3.5 Flash at 41.1% got only +7.1 pp, but Gemini 3.1 Pro at 36.0% got +24.8 pp. Ordering is weakly consistent; harness and model are confounded. New: a pre-registered GAIA study found the strongest Anthropic model gained most from structure at Level 2 (gap 0.28 vs Haiku 0.26), while an observational study of 19 coding agents found the framework effect shrank 19.4 -> 3.8 -> 0.9 pp over three Claude generations. Evidence points both ways.
agent_test: Hold harness fixed, vary model strength; regress lift on baseline.

claim: Help the agent writes for itself hurts under the v4 protocol: self-generated skills -8.1, -11.3, -11.5 pp on three frontier configurations (87 tasks). The v1 protocol (same-session writing, 84 tasks, other models) gave -1.3 pp on average, so these are different methods, not a revision. Trajectory audit: packs unused (10 of 12 audited), authoring displaces solving, used packs lock in confident errors.
agent_test: Do not add self-written scaffolds without a verifier; test self-made vs fixed hint at equal tokens.

claim: More help is not better: 1 skill +18.0, 2-3 skills +19.0, 4+ skills +10.1 pp; comprehensive docs +0.7 vs compact +19.0 pp (observational). Generic extra rules cut a small model on RAG from 26/30 to 9/30, and few-shot over-prompting shows a peak then decline. Fits an extraneous-load reading.
agent_test: Vary scaffold length at fixed content; report accuracy per token; ablate each guardrail.
audit_note: SkillsBench (full text) and Commey numbers match; the GPT models in Tang et al. showed no significant drop, and the Qwen 9/30 drop was one prompt condition, so 'peak then decline' holds only for smaller open models.

claim: Chain-of-thought (added support) helps mainly math and symbolic tasks (avg +14.2 symbolic, +12.3 math, +6.9 logic) and little elsewhere, and can hurt where deliberation hurts humans (up to -36.3 pp o1-preview vs GPT-4o). Abstract-level check: the 36.3 figure confirmed, the 95% equals-sign figure not seen in the abstract.
agent_test: Switch deliberation on only for task types where it paid off in a calibration set.
audit_note: Numbers match Sprague (14.2/12.3/6.9) and Liu (36.3 point drop); the 95% equals-sign figure is in the Sprague abstract-adjacent text (as much as 95% of MMLU gain).

claim: A reasoning-trained model reported worse results with few-shot examples (a model-side reversal); the vendor gave no ablation table.
agent_test: Test few-shot exemplars on a strong reasoning model vs a weak one.

claim: In a 131-learner study of an LLM tutor (Hou et al. 2026), of 515 coded fading episodes only 282 followed a learner's answer to the tutor's question (the rest followed a pasted plan or code, a bare 'it's fine', or other content), so learner uptake of questions was limited; in simulated dialogs with RL-trained tutors using a solution-handover gate, the supplying-answers move fell from 15.5% to 2.2% (Macina et al. 2026).
agent_test: Make fading depend on the measured pass rate of recent attempts, not on a script.
audit_note: In Hou et al. the 282 of 515 are fading episodes that followed a learner's answer to the tutor's question (not a tutor 'direct answer'), the paper presents contingency as working, and it covers one tutor design; Macina's 15.5 to 2.2 is the supplying-answers move rate after RL in simulated dialogs.
claim_before_audit: Tutor fading in LLM tutoring is poorly contingent: only 282 of 515 coded fading episodes followed a direct answer. Tutors trained to withhold answers cut answer supplying from 15.5% to 2.2% in simulation.

claim: Assistance-dilemma training in simulation: ablating gates left transfer gain nearly unchanged (+0.23 vs +0.25) but raised answer leak from 31% to 61%. Student was an 8B LLM, judge an LLM.
agent_test: Measure leakage of the answer into the scaffold on our agent.

claim: AI-generated help can hurt strong LLM learners: SLATE slide effects were positive for most student models, but a strong-baseline deck dropped from 70% to 40%. Cause unproven (format shift), so it may not be expertise reversal.
agent_test: Check for format-induced shift when adding scaffolds on high-baseline items.

claim: Delaying help improved hint-writing quality for 97 graduate students (beta 1.096 deferred vs 0.75 on-demand AI).
agent_test: Agent attempts first and sees help only after a failed attempt; compare to help-first.

claim: LLM-based adaptive training showed no expertise moderation in a large field trial: condition x tenure interaction b=0 in N=2,574; overall knowledge d about 0.29.
agent_test: Do not assume moderation; measure it on our agent.

claim: No registered replication of the founding studies was found. The 2025 meta-analysis found no publication-bias signal (Egger p=.57, .77). Partial or null results exist outside the founding network (law reasoning, a retention-vs-transfer split) but were seen only as snippets.
agent_test: Treat the effect as a prior and test on our own agent.

claim: The size of the reversal depends on how far apart the groups are. It is strongest when novice and expert groups differ by grade level or profession, and weak when one sample is split by a short knowledge test (expert side net about -0.2 versus -0.95 for grade level). It is also weak in primary school and in language and humanities.
agent_test: Do not expect much harm from help on a within-model split; test the effect at a large capability gap (small vs frontier model) instead.

claim: No controlled study has crossed scaffold strength with model strength at equal tokens. Closest: a pre-registered GAIA study (3 scaffolds, 5 models) rejected 'stronger models need less scaffold' at Level 2 and found model family matters; an observational coding-agent study found the scaffold gain fell from 19.4 to 0.9 pp across Claude generations.
agent_test: Run one harness, two to three model sizes, schema strength at 3 levels, matched total tokens, tasks split by difficulty.

claim: An adaptive trigger for fading has a human template (rapid test of expertise correlating up to .92 with a full test; performance plus load rating chose the next step and beat a yoked control) and a design argument (assess knowledge repeatedly). No tested rule exists for LLM loops. Class pass rate from few tasks cannot locate a threshold (n=10, 8/10 has CI 0.49 to 0.94).
agent_test: Compare three triggers (running class pass rate, per-item verifier probe, fixed schedule) at matched tokens.

claim: Element interactivity can be set and counted for synthetic reasoning tasks (CogniLoad: number of interacting entities and attributes; accuracy falls with it in all 22 models, with a per-model threshold), but nobody has shown it predicts scaffold benefit in agents.
agent_test: Tag our tasks by jointly-held constraints, fit scaffold benefit on that count and on baseline pass rate, and compare the fits.

claim: Extra worked experience can hurt a strong agent and the sign depends on model and effort: seven tutorial levels lowered AGI Maze scores for both GPT-5.5 variants at both effort settings, helped GPT-5.6-sol at xhigh and were mixed at max.
agent_test: Test exemplars per model and per effort setting, not once.
